{"id": "23:35/q14", "question": "Where else does the Quran present the objection about reviving dust and bones?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:35/q14/p1", "position": "The same objection recurs in several verses, with other passages addressing revival of dead bones.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 17:49, 17:98, 23:82, 37:16, 37:53, and 56:47 for the recurring objection, and 36:78 and 79:11 for dead bones being revived."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q01", "question": "What does هي refer to, and how is its referent understood?", "turns_on": "Whether the following predicate serves as a backward antecedent or clarifies a referent already present in context or thought; al-Samin also disputes a proposed technical classification of the former.", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q01/p1", "position": "It refers to life, supplied or identified by the following predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Thalabi, al-Baghawi and al-Wahidi identify the referent as worldly life. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi reconstruct an underlying 'there is no life except our worldly life': the predicate identifies the replaced noun. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi cite the line 'hiya al-nafs ma hammaltaha tatahammal'; al-Alusi adds 'hiya al-Arab taqulu ma sha'at' as backward-reference parallels. Al-Baydawi says replacement avoids repetition and suggests the identity is evident. Al-Alusi answers an objection that the qualified predicate would make the reference tautological: the pronoun can refer to the noun without its qualification. Ibn Ashur describes deliberate initial vagueness followed by explanatory apposition, and rules out a pronoun of the story because a singular noun, rather than a clause, explains it and the construction precludes that analysis."}, {"id": "23:37/q01/p2", "position": "It refers to life already understood from the context or as a familiar mental concept; the following words clarify it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan derives the referent from the preceding mockery of resurrection. Al-Samin says context explains the pronoun and rejects calling al-Zamakhshari's analysis explanation by what follows in both wording and syntax. Al-Alusi prefers the mentally understood genus of life; al-Kashf compares a familiar concept indicated by what follows to 'this is your brother'."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q02", "question": "What claim does إِنْ هِىَ إِلَّا حَيَاتُنَا ٱلدُّنْيَا make?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q02/p1", "position": "The present worldly life is the only life; no life follows death.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi calls it the near, present life; al-Tabrisi the familiar one. Al-Bursevi calls it near and perishing, and Ibn Ashur says dunya is the nearer life. Al-Biqai says their emphatic dismissal of resurrection leads to this claim. Elmalili reports their reasoning from the supposed impossibility of bodily resurrection from dust and bones to enjoying this low life. Asad says they also accuse the messenger of lying about God."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q03", "question": "How does إِنْ form the negation here?", "turns_on": "Whether the particle is described by its genus-negating force or by equivalence to negative ma; the notes do not present these descriptions as mutually exclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q03/p1", "position": "The negative in applies to a pronoun denoting the genus of life, with the force of la negating the entire genus.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain the genus-wide force; al-Alusi's preferred mental-genus analysis likewise yields no life except worldly life. Al-Samarrai points to earlier discussion of differences among negating particles while citing this and parallel formulations, without specifying a further analysis here."}, {"id": "23:37/q03/p2", "position": "In is a negative particle meaning ma, making the clause a restriction to worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi explicitly equates negative in with ma."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q04", "question": "What does ٱلدُّنْيَا add to the description of life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q04/p1", "position": "It is the near, present worldly life, which passes away.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi calls it near and present; al-Bursevi adds that it perishes; Ibn Ashur glosses it as nearer, present life."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q05", "question": "What does نَمُوتُ وَنَحْيَا mean, and how does its order work?", "turns_on": "Whether dying and living refer to successive generations, coexisting people, the same person's ordinary life, prior lifelessness, a continued life through descendants, or return through transmigration; some accounts instead explain or alter the word order.", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q05/p1", "position": "One generation dies and a new generation is born in its place.", "reasons": "Muqatil describes an endless cycle; Ibn Zayd compares generations to harvested and sprouting crops and cites deniers in 34:7 and 34:3. Yahya ibn Sallam says they die and are born. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Biqai, al-Alusi and al-Tabatabai likewise explain replacement. Al-Samin rejects using the word order as proof that waw lacks sequence, because successive replacement itself explains it. Al-Alusi says individual return would contradict their denial. Al-Tabatabai prefers this contextual reading to transmigration. Ibn Ashur allows that the living continue until their own deaths, alongside successive births."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p2", "position": "Fathers or ancestors die while their children or descendants live on.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi reports Mujahid's sequence of children then descendants, with al-Kalbi and Muqatil agreeing; al-Mawardi and al-Tabrisi attribute the father-child detail to al-Kalbi. Al-Alusi regards the stronger suggestion that children's survival counts as their parents' continued life as far-fetched."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p3", "position": "Some people die while others remain alive, without specifying new births or family descent.", "reasons": "Ibn Isa and the anonymous reports distinguish this general coexistence from specific generational and father-child explanations. Al-Razi says this excludes any individual's return; Ibn Ashur adds that survivors continue only until they too die."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p4", "position": "It describes each person's ordinary worldly life followed by death, with the verbal order reversed in meaning.", "reasons": "Ibn Shajara and others paraphrase it as 'we live and die.' Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Ashur say waw need not impose chronology. Al-Qurtubi cites the paired commands in 3:43; al-Alusi cites a proposed parallel in 3:55. Al-Bursevi and Study Quran's R describe only this world's life and death. Al-Samin objects to using this verse itself to prove waw lacks sequence, since successive generations already explain the surface order."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p5", "position": "Dying means an individual's prior lifelessness, followed by birth and worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj speaks of humans beginning as lifeless matter, then living and dying. Al-Qurtubi specifies lifeless drops of semen before life. Al-Alusi finds the explanation from prebirth nonexistence far-fetched."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p6", "position": "Their children staying alive is counted figuratively as the dead parents' continued life.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this proposal but regards it as far-fetched."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p7", "position": "The speakers actually meant that they die and then themselves live again.", "reasons": "Al-Samin reports this interpretation of return to life after death without specifying a mechanism; al-Alusi says individual return conflicts with the explicit denial of resurrection."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p8", "position": "It can describe transmigration: souls leave dead bodies and enter newly formed bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi does not find this proposal far-fetched. Al-Tabatabai says it was common among idolaters, could include human or nonhuman bodies and was called 'birth after birth,' but fits the context poorly."}, {"id": "23:37/q05/p9", "position": "They may have actually said 'we live and die,' while the quoted order was changed to suit the preceding clause.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi distinguishes a change in the report of their speech from merely treating waw as temporally unordered."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q06", "question": "Is there a reported variant order for نَمُوتُ وَنَحْيَا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q06/p1", "position": "Ubayy and Ibn Masud read 'we live and die' in the reverse order.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi attributes the reversed reading to both Ubayy and Ibn Masud."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q07", "question": "What do the speakers deny by وَمَا نَحْنُ بِمَبْعُوثِينَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q07/p1", "position": "They deny being raised after death for an afterlife and judgment.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd compares their denial with that of opponents in 34:7 and 34:3. Al-Baghawi adds being spread abroad after death; Abu Hayyan specifies resurrection for judgment. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan associate the denial with the unbelief of the materialist eternalists. Al-Bursevi counters their blindness by saying restoration is easier than initial creation and the creator of existence and nonexistence can restore life; he attributes the claim to Hud's people. Elmalili says they consider bodily resurrection from dust and bones impossibly remote. Asad says they also accuse the messenger of inventing lies."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q08", "question": "How does the wording strengthen the final denial of resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q08/p1", "position": "Its coordinated nominal form makes the denial sustained and emphatic.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the final clause makes the denial continuous and emphatic. Ibn Ashur says coordination follows the restriction to immediate life and death, while nominal wording strengthens the assertion."}]}

{"id": "23:37/q11", "question": "What does the chiefs' rejection reveal about their stance?", "turns_on": "Al-Jishumi highlights inconsistency in their argument; Kuranyolu explains the social interest behind opposition.", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q11/p1", "position": "Their objection is inconsistent because they call following a living messenger loss while worshipping powerless, inanimate idols.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi contrasts the alleged loss in obeying the messenger with their unquestioned idol worship: idols neither help nor harm."}, {"id": "23:37/q11/p2", "position": "Powerful, affluent opponents fear afterlife accountability and a just society that would threaten their interests.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says they benefit from the prevailing order and fear public awareness of universal rights and justice."}]}
{"id": "23:37/q12", "question": "How does the denial fit the surah's wider pattern?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:37/q12/p1", "position": "It belongs to the surah's recurring accounts of prophets facing rejection, often from affluent and powerful opponents.", "reasons": "Study Quran says the surah moves from worldly blessings to Noah's denial and rebuke by his people and his ark journey. {"id": "23:41/q01", "question": "How does the seizure follow the messenger's plea and the surrounding account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q01/p1", "position": "The initial fa marks the prompt answer to the messenger's prayer and the fulfillment of God's promise.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the fa as prompt response; al-Biqāʿī connects the destruction with Noah's prayer and God's promise to him."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q02", "question": "Who were the people seized by the cry?", "turns_on": "Whether the cry and neighboring details identify Thamūd, the succession after Noah identifies ʿĀd, or the lack of names makes the account general; ʿĀd's wind destruction needs reconciliation with the cry.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q02/p1", "position": "They were Thamūd, Ṣāliḥ's people.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and al-Ṭabarī name Thamūd; al-Bayḍāwī names Ṣāliḥ's people. Ibn ʿĀshūr favors this from the cry or thunderbolt, morning regret and surviving ruins at al-Ḥijr (23:40; 15:83; 37:137–38). Al-Sāmarrāʾī takes the definite 'the people' here as Ṣāliḥ's nation, versus indefinite 'a people' in 23:44. Al-Biqāʿī and al-Bursawī relate the literal cry especially to Thamūd."}, {"id": "23:41/q02/p2", "position": "They were ʿĀd, Hūd's people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports the view that the generation succeeded Noah's people; Kuranyolu says most commentators identify ʿĀd and Hūd. Al-Bursawī also cites the heavenly cry that destroyed Shaddād and his family near Iram."}, {"id": "23:41/q02/p3", "position": "The generation is left unnamed to describe the recurring experience of messengers and rejecting peoples.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu reports Esed's general reading and adopts it. Ibn ʿĀshūr says unnamed generations illustrate the recurring fate of deniers, while the specific identity can still be inferred."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q03", "question": "What was the cry that seized them?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣayḥa names an audible destructive event, an earthquake or thunderbolt, or figuratively the punishment or death it brought; the reported wind destruction of ʿĀd affects the literal reading.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q03/p1", "position": "It was a literal deadly shout, usually Gabriel's single cry.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Bayḍāwī and others say Gabriel's shout killed everyone, sometimes by bursting or splitting their hearts; al-Jishumī also reports an unnamed angel. Al-Qurṭubī pairs Gabriel's cry with wind; Ibn Kathīr reports a violent cold wind leaving houses (46:25); al-Ālūsī allows Gabriel's cry within wind. Al-Bursawī defines ṣayḥa as a raised voice. Rāzī prefers this literal reading."}, {"id": "23:41/q03/p2", "position": "It was an earthquake or great quaking.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit this from Ibn ʿAbbās; the Study Quran reports the quaking interpretation."}, {"id": "23:41/q03/p3", "position": "It was the sound of a thunderbolt.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr favors this because the thunderbolt and cry descriptions of Thamūd fit together (69:5; 15:83)."}, {"id": "23:41/q03/p4", "position": "The cry denotes punishment or overwhelming torment.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan, al-Baghawī, al-Jishumī, Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī report this explanation; a poetic cry against the Barmakids illustrates overwhelming disaster. Al-Jishumī and al-Baghawī also give destruction itself. Al-Biqāʿī allows figurative terrible punishment. One Abū Ḥayyān poetic line depicts a cry throwing people on their chins."}, {"id": "23:41/q03/p5", "position": "The cry denotes death itself.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan likens it to someone being called and answering; Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bursawī and the Study Quran include death among the interpretations."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q04", "question": "How does the cry 'take' them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q04/p1", "position": "Taking them means destroying them, with the cry named as the cause or accompaniment of destruction.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls 'taking' a metaphor for destruction and the attribution to the cry a rational metaphor: the sound caused destruction or accompanied the air tearing when a thunderbolt fell."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q05", "question": "What does 'in truth' say about their seizure?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥaqq emphasizes moral justice, an unavoidable reality or decree, fulfillment of a true warning, divine command, or several of these senses together.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q05/p1", "position": "The seizure was just punishment earned by disbelief, denial, and wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says vengeance followed disbelief and denial of the messenger; Ibn ʿAbbās says they denied truth. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds their deeds and God's decree; Rāzī and al-Nasafī compare judging by truth to judging justly. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the bāʾ marks accompaniment, with justice rather than assault. Ibn Kathīr cites disbelief and tyranny; the Study Quran and Asad likewise stress justice."}, {"id": "23:41/q05/p2", "position": "It was an established and irresistible reality or decree.", "reasons": "Al-Mufaḍḍal cites death's stupor arriving 'with truth' (50:19). {"id": "23:41/q07", "question": "What does making them like ghuthāʾ convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q07/p1", "position": "They were killed and reduced to lifeless, worthless remains like debris cast about by a flood.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says the debris has no use and Ibn Zayd calls this a divine simile; Ibn Qutayba notes it disperses. {"id": "23:41/q11", "question": "What does buʿdan mean for the wrongdoers?", "turns_on": "Whether remoteness is explained chiefly as death and destruction or as exclusion from divine mercy and good; several sources give both.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q11/p1", "position": "It means destruction, ruin or perdition.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī, Rāzī and al-Nasafī gloss it as their perishing; al-Naqqāsh stresses increased ruin and punishment. Al-Biqāʿī includes expulsion; al-Ālūsī notes the second verb form for destruction. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the opposite idiom lā tabʿad, 'do not be lost,' in Mālik ibn al-Rayb's burial poem; al-Wāḥidī compares Midian's curse in 11:95."}, {"id": "23:41/q11/p2", "position": "It means distance from God's mercy, good or salvation, like a curse.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĪsā, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Kāshifī specify exclusion from mercy. Rāzī adds scorn and greater exclusion from bliss in the Hereafter after worldly punishment; al-Ālūsī includes good and salvation. Al-Jishumī compares suḥqan and the opposite lā tabʿad in poetry."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q12", "question": "Is fa-buʿdan a report or a curse?", "turns_on": "Whether the form invokes distance upon them or declares the distance and ruin already realized.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q12/p1", "position": "It is an imprecation or denunciation against them.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī treats it like suḥqan and contrasts lā tabʿad; al-Ṭabarī asks that God drive the deniers away. Rāzī says God uses it to humiliate and warn later generations; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it is a curse and rebuke, not a literal prayer for people already dead. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ allows curse, denunciation and supplication."}, {"id": "23:41/q12/p2", "position": "It reports or declares that their doom and distance have occurred.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says God imposed remoteness; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī explicitly allow a statement of their ruin or distance as well as a curse."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q13", "question": "How is buʿdan parsed and vocalized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q13/p1", "position": "It is an accusative verbal noun replacing a verb whose governor is omitted.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Samīn require the unspoken verb; Rāzī cites Sībawayh for buʿdan, suḥqan and damran. Al-Qurṭubī compares 'watering' and 'tending'; al-Bursawī says its expressed governor is rare. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares tabban and suḥqan. Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn note fatḥa or sukūn on ʿayn and analogous forms of rashada."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q14", "question": "What does the lām in lil-qawmi attach to?", "turns_on": "Whether the lām has an unspoken explanatory attachment or is governed directly by buʿdan; al-Samīn disputes attestation for the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q14/p1", "position": "It attaches to an omitted explanatory expression specifying those cursed.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr give this analysis; al-Samīn compares suqyā lahu and jadʿan lahu, and says fa-taʿsan lahum (47:8) gives no support for direct attachment."}, {"id": "23:41/q14/p2", "position": "It attaches directly to buʿdan, indicating for whom distance is invoked.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān transmits al-Ḥawfī's analysis. {"id": "23:41/q15", "question": "Who are 'the wrongdoing people' and why this description?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is read with focus on the identified deniers in the episode or on the comprehensive warning that extends to people like them.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q15/p1", "position": "They are the polytheist deniers who wronged themselves and resisted their messenger.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī call them polytheists; Ibn ʿAbbās calls them deniers. {"id": "23:41/q16", "question": "Why name the wrongdoing people instead of using a pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q16/p1", "position": "The explicit description identifies those condemned, gives their wrongdoing as the cause, and extends the warning.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says the noun replaces their pronoun to supply the reason; al-Ālūsī agrees. {"id": "23:41/q17", "question": "What wider warning or lesson does this destruction convey?", "turns_on": "Whether attention falls on the recurring warning to rejecters or on the contrast between their end and believers' survival.", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q17/p1", "position": "Deniers of messengers deserve destruction after proof; the account warns later rejecters and shows God's recurring pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says sending messengers removes excuses before deserved punishment. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects coincidence and the Study Quran notes recurring opposition of affluent and powerful people (7:59–62, 7:136)."}, {"id": "23:41/q17/p2", "position": "The messenger and believers were saved and prospered, inheriting the land while the unbelievers perished.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī makes this the counterpart to the destruction."}]}
{"id": "23:41/q18", "question": "What theological point is drawn from sending the messenger before destruction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q18/p1", "position": "The sending of messengers establishes proof and human accountability, opposing the claim that God creates all human acts.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī argues that if God created all acts, sending messengers would have no purpose; he applies this to compulsion, capacity and will."}]}

{"id": "23:41/q21", "question": "What is suḥaq, the curse word compared with buʿdan?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:41/q21/p1", "position": "Suḥaq is a valley in Hell.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr calls it a valley in Hell and distinguishes Saʿīr as a valley of pus; al-Suyūṭī lists Suḥaq among several named valleys of Hell."}]}
{"id": "23:71/q01", "question": "Who or what is al-ḥaqq here?", "turns_on": "Whether al-ḥaqq names God, the revealed message, or truth and reality itself; Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects to the divine referent, while al-Ālūsī defends its contextual fit.", "positions": [{"id": "23:71/q01/p1", "position": "God Himself.", "reasons": "Reported by Abū Ṣāliḥ, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddī, Mujāhid, Qatāda and others; al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī call this the majority view. Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects that God has permitted unbelief to continue without cosmic collapse, so the verb and consequence are difficult."}, {"id": "23:71/q01/p2", "position": "The Qur’an, revelation, Islam, or the truth brought by Muḥammad.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj connects revelation to 23:70; al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj are cited by al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, and Ibn al-Jawzī. Ṭabāṭabāʾī grounds truth in the cosmic order and fitrah (30:30); Asad takes all created reality; Kur'an Yolu includes universal law and balance."}, {"id": "23:71/q01/p4", "position": "Unity and justice as inward realities.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls truth the summons to Essence and attributes: unity sustains immaterial reality and its shadow, justice, orders the multiplicity of heaven and earth."}]}
{"id": "23:71/q02", "question": "What does following their desires mean in this condition?", "turns_on": "The notes variously construe following as divine action or legislation, conformity of reality or revelation, or the Prophet's hypothetical response.", "positions": [{"id": "23:71/q02/p1", "position": "Truth or reality would agree with their wishes, especially their wish for shirk.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls following a familiar metaphor for agreement; al-Qurṭubī also gives metaphorical agreement, including impunity through supposed divine incapacity or ignorance. Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers this over God as subject. The Study Quran reports this wording; al-Ālūsī distinguishes truth in general from truth about divinity."}, {"id": "23:71/q02/p2", "position": "God would act or legislate according to their desire for partners, offspring, shirk or sins.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Kalbī describe God taking a partner; al-Baghawī adds a son; al-Zamakhsharī describes commanding shirk and sin. Ibn Kathīr points to conflicting human opinions and God's perfect governance. Al-Ālūsī says this is impossible but contextually apt."}, {"id": "23:71/q02/p3", "position": "The Qur’an or revelation would descend endorsing their wishes.", "reasons": "Their wishes include partners, offspring and other deities, according to al-Wāḥidī and al-Baghawī; al-Wāḥidī says this would reverse its call to good. Al-Ālūsī also paraphrases it as the Prophet bringing shirk rather than his revealed message."}, {"id": "23:71/q02/p4", "position": "Their desires concern what they wish for.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this as one scope of ahwāʾihim, alongside their worship."}, {"id": "23:71/q02/p5", "position": "Their desires concern what they worship.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this as the other scope of ahwāʾihim."}]}
{"id": "23:71/q03", "question": "Whose desires are meant, and what counts as desire?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is limited to appetites or includes corrupt choices and wishes contrary to nature.", "positions": [{"id": "23:71/q03/p1", "position": "The desires of the Meccan polytheists and unbelievers.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā explicitly identifies the polytheists; Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī identify Meccan unbelievers or polytheists. Their particular wishes include partners, offspring, idolatry and denial of Muḥammad."}, {"id": "23:71/q03/p2", "position": "Hawā is desire for one's own purpose, especially an unwarranted or corrupt appetite.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr excludes ordinary hunger and thirst as such; examples are injustice, humiliation, stolen food and illicit sex. Islahi says human desire and truth make incompatible demands."}]}
{"id": "23:71/q04", "question": "Why would the heavens and earth be corrupted?", "turns_on": "The causal account ranges from impossible multiple gods, through conflicting whims and moral disorder, to immediate destruction or loss of divinity.", "positions": [{"id": "23:71/q04/p1", "position": "Multiple gods or endorsing shirk would undo cosmic governance.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī invoke 21:22; Islahi invokes 23:91, where each god takes its creation and attacks another. Al-Biqāʿī describes mutual obstruction. Al-Ālūsī reports the objection that Quraysh's shirk in worship did not imply rival lordship, citing 31:25."}, {"id": "23:71/q04/p2", "position": "Conflicting, vicious or unstable desires would destroy the true order that sustains creation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says people lack foresight and favor falsehood; al-Qaffāl says their opinions contradict each other. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī say proofs, justified conclusions and trust in promises and threats would fail. Ibn Kathīr cites their disagreements, comparing God's perfect attributes and rule (43:31–32, 17:100, 4:53). Ibn ʿĀshūr includes moral wrongs such as infanticide, killing and gambling. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says fitrah, cosmic causes and relations would have to turn arbitrary. Kur'an Yolu gives the example that proper work succeeds even for an unbeliever, whereas poor work can fail even for a believer. Islahi lists vice, injustice and denial of Judgment. Al-Ālūsī dismisses one contradictory-desires formulation."}, {"id": "23:71/q04/p3", "position": "God would bring the Resurrection and end the world in anger if Muhammad's truth became shirk.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī offer this consequence; al-Ālūsī calls the supposition that revelation could be changed impossible."}, {"id": "23:71/q04/p4", "position": "God commanding shirk and sin would cease to be God and could not sustain the cosmos.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī's explanation is repeated by Abū Ḥayyān; al-Bayḍāwī calls it a Muʿtazilite principle. Al-Khafājī, reported by al-Ālūsī, says reason establishes that such legislation is a divine deficiency."}, {"id": "23:71/q04/p5", "position": "A purposeless, meaningless universe such as deniers imagine could not endure.", "reasons": "Asad says the universe, especially human life, would perish in chaos under this assumption."}, {"id": "23:71/q04/p6", "position": "The heavens' and earth's governance would be corrupted.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī contrasts governance by truth with governance by whim; Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds that creation and command, existence and governance, are inseparable."}, {"id": "23:71/q04/p7", "position": "Their conditions would be corrupted.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says cosmic conditions proceed by wisdom, not whim."}]}
{"id": "23:71/q05", "question": "Who are those 'within them,' and how would they be affected?", "turns_on": "Whether man singles out rational inhabitants or includes creatures between heaven and earth, including animals and inanimate things.", "positions": [{"id": "23:71/q05/p1", "position": "Rational inhabitants: angels in heaven, humans on earth, and sometimes jinn.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī names angels and humans; al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Burṣawī include jinn. {"id": "23:71/q11", "question": "What is 'their reminder'?", "turns_on": "Whether dhikr stresses honor, admonition and guidance, clarification, duties and recompense, or the book they once wished to receive.", "positions": [{"id": "23:71/q11/p1", "position": "The Qur’an as their honor, renown and distinction.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī and Sufyān link it to the messenger from their people and Qur’an in their language; 21:10 and 43:44 are repeatedly cited.
